choices: A boolean saying whether the exception was thrown or not
The thrown exception, so its message can be checked too
Nothing; it only prints the exception's stack trace to the console
The message string, or null when nothing was thrown
quiz.explanation: assertThrows fails the test when nothing is thrown or another type is thrown. Otherwise it returns the exception, typed as IllegalArgumentException, so the next line can assert on its message. It is not a boolean check and it prints nothing; a test that only needs to know the call failed can ignore the returned value.

quiz.prompt: `List<Order> findOpen()` on a Mockito mock was never stubbed. What does a call return?
choices: null, like every other unstubbed method
It throws UnsupportedOperationException
A list that holds one mock Order
An empty list, not null
quiz.explanation: Mockito's default answer gives an empty list for a List return type, Optional.empty() for Optional, 0 or false for primitives and wrappers, and null only for other object types. An unstubbed call never throws UnsupportedOperationException and never invents a mock Order, so code that loops over the result just sees no open orders.

quiz.prompt: The test stubs `when(repo.findByEmail("ana@x.io")).thenReturn(Optional.of(ana))`. The code calls `repo.findByEmail("ANA@x.io")`. What does it get?
choices: Optional.empty(): the arguments are matched with equals
Optional.of(ana), because stubs ignore letter case
An exception, since the call matches no stub
null, because the stub has no default value
quiz.explanation: Arguments are compared with equals, and "ANA@x.io" is not equal to "ana@x.io", so the call gets the default answer for an Optional return type.

quiz.prompt: Which dependency is the best candidate for a Mockito mock or a hand-written fake?
choices: A JDBC ResultSet, so that the test needs no database at all
Your own PaymentGateway interface around the card provider
The BigDecimal arithmetic inside the price calculator
The JPA EntityManager that the repository calls into
quiz.explanation: Fake the boundary you own. Third-party types like ResultSet and EntityManager should be tested against the real thing, and plain arithmetic needs no double at all.

quiz.prompt: Why is mocking `EntityManager` in a repository test risky?
choices: Mockito cannot mock interfaces that come from the jakarta packages
Its methods are final, so every stub is silently ignored by Mockito
It encodes your guess of JPA, and a wrong guess still passes
The test would need a whole running Spring context
quiz.explanation: A mock of a type you do not own tests your assumptions about it. A repository test against a real database finds the query, mapping and flush problems the mock hides.

quiz.prompt: A test stubs five methods, calls the service, then verifies all five calls in order. What is the main problem?
choices: verify has no way to check the order in which calls happened
Five stubs make Mockito noticeably slower on every run
It mirrors the implementation, so every refactor breaks it
A stubbed method can no longer be verified
quiz.explanation: The test restates how the service works instead of what it promises, so merging or renaming two internal calls breaks it while a wrong result can still pass. Assert on the outcome and verify only the interactions that are the behaviour, such as one receipt. Speed is not the issue, and InOrder can check order when order matters.

quiz.prompt: A test writes `when(spy.loadAll()).thenReturn(List.of())` on a spy whose real `loadAll` calls the network. What happens?
choices: The stub takes effect and nothing real runs at any point
The real loadAll runs once while the stub is set up
Mockito refuses, because a spy can never be stubbed at all
The spy turns into a plain mock for every one of its methods
quiz.explanation: when(spy.loadAll()) has to call spy.loadAll() to know what to stub, and on a spy that is the real method. doReturn(...).when(spy).loadAll() stubs without calling it.

quiz.prompt: Many tests will share a payment fake. Which behaviour should it keep from the real gateway?
choices: None: a fake should simply approve every charge it gets
A random delay on every call, so tests feel realistic
A reused idempotency key returns the first charge
A console log line for every call, to help debugging
quiz.explanation: The fake must keep the rules the code relies on. Idempotency is what makes a retry after a timeout safe, so a fake without it cannot test that retry.

quiz.prompt: With `MockitoExtension`'s strict stubs, a test stubs a method that the code under test never calls. What happens?
choices: The test fails with an unnecessary-stubbing error
Nothing at all: unused stubs are simply ignored
The stub carries over into the next test method
Mockito logs a warning and the test passes
quiz.explanation: MockitoExtension uses strict stubs by default, so a stub the code never calls fails the test with an unnecessary-stubbing error once the test ends. It is not simply ignored or downgraded to a warning, and it cannot carry over, because every test gets fresh mocks. An unused stub usually means the test or the code is not doing what its author thinks.

flashcards.back: By default a new instance of the test class is created for every test method, so instance fields start fresh in each test.
@BeforeEach runs before every test method; @BeforeAll runs once for the class and is a static method by default.
Unstubbed calls return null for most objects, zero or false for primitives and wrappers, and empty collections, Optional or streams for those types.

flashcards.front: How does Mockito match a stub's arguments?
flashcards.back: With equals on each argument, unless matchers are used, and then every argument of that call must be a matcher.
Stub to supply the inputs a test needs; verify only the interactions that are themselves the behaviour, such as one receipt email.

flashcards.front: Don't mock what you don't own
flashcards.back: Mock or fake your own interfaces at the boundary, and test third-party types such as JDBC or JPA against the real thing.
Use doReturn(value).when(spy).method(), because when(spy.method()) runs the real method while setting up the stub.
It keeps the real dependency's rules, such as idempotency keys and declines, so tests fail where production would fail.

topics.title: Spring Security basics: the filter chain & method security
topics.summary: How the security filter chain sits in front of every controller, first-match authorization rules and Ant patterns, the thread-local SecurityContext, how ExceptionTranslationFilter chooses 401 or 403, the ROLE_ prefix behind hasRole, proxy-based method security, and when CSRF protection applies.
topics.lesson:
## The filter chain runs before your controller

Every request passes through the servlet filters before `DispatcherServlet` picks a controller. Spring Security installs one filter, `FilterChainProxy`, which hands the request to the FIRST `SecurityFilterChain` whose matcher fits it and runs that chain's filters in order: CSRF protection, the authentication filters (bearer token, form login, HTTP Basic), `ExceptionTranslationFilter`, and `AuthorizationFilter` last. A request refused there never reaches your code.

```java
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/health").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .build();
}
```

## Rules are checked in order: the first match wins

`authorizeHttpRequests` tries its rules from top to bottom and applies the first one that matches the request; later rules are never consulted. Put specific paths before general ones and `anyRequest()` last (Spring refuses a rule added after `anyRequest()`). A `/**` rule placed above `/api/admin/**` decides admin paths too. In these Ant-style patterns `*` matches exactly one path segment and `**` any number of segments, so `/api/**` also matches `/api` itself.

## Who is calling: the SecurityContext

An authentication filter that accepts the credentials stores an `Authentication` (the principal and its granted authorities) in the `SecurityContextHolder`. By default that holder is thread-local: code running on another thread, such as a plain executor or an `@Async` method, does not see the user unless the context is propagated (`DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor`). The framework clears the context when the request ends, so a pooled thread never carries one user's identity into the next request.

## 401 or 403: ExceptionTranslationFilter decides

When the authorization filter refuses a request, `ExceptionTranslationFilter` turns the exception into a response. An `AuthenticationException`, or an `AccessDeniedException` while the caller is still anonymous, starts authentication through the `AuthenticationEntryPoint`: 401 with `WWW-Authenticate` for an API, a redirect to the login page for form login. An `AccessDeniedException` for an authenticated caller goes to the `AccessDeniedHandler`: 403.

## Roles are authorities with a prefix

`hasRole("ADMIN")` checks for the granted authority `ROLE_ADMIN`; `hasAuthority("orders:write")` checks the exact string. A user granted plain `ADMIN` therefore fails every `hasRole("ADMIN")` rule. The reverse mistake is caught early: `hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN")` is refused when the chain is built, because the prefix is added for you. Pick one convention and keep it in the code that builds the authorities, for example the converter that turns a JWT's `scope` claim into `SCOPE_orders:write` authorities.

## Method security goes through a proxy

`@EnableMethodSecurity` activates `@PreAuthorize` on bean methods: `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")`, or `@PreAuthorize("#ownerId == authentication.name")` to compare a parameter with the caller. Like `@Transactional` (topic 20) it is applied by a proxy around the bean, so a call from inside the same bean (`this.deleteAll()`) skips the check entirely.

## CSRF protection

CSRF protection is on by default in every chain that `HttpSecurity` builds: a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE that does not carry the CSRF token is refused with 403, while GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are left alone. It matters wherever the browser attaches the credential by itself, which is what a session cookie is. A stateless API that authenticates every request with a bearer token in the `Authorization` header does not need it, because a browser never adds that header to a cross-site request on its own; `oauth2ResourceServer` already skips the CSRF check for requests that carry a bearer token.

quiz.prompt: A request to `/api/orders` carries no credentials, and the matching rule is `authenticated()`. Where is it stopped?
choices: In the security filter chain, before any controller runs
In the controller, by an if statement on the current user
In the DispatcherServlet, while it picks a handler
At the database, when the query finds no matching user
quiz.explanation: FilterChainProxy is a servlet filter in front of DispatcherServlet, and AuthorizationFilter at the end of the chain refuses the anonymous request there, so no handler is ever picked. No if statement in your own code is involved, and no database is asked about a user: credentials that were never sent cannot be looked up.

quiz.prompt: The rules are `.requestMatchers("/**").authenticated()` and then `.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`. A signed-in non-admin requests `/admin/users`. What happens?
choices: 403, because the more specific admin rule takes precedence
The app fails at startup because two rules overlap
Allowed: the first matching rule, /**, decides
401, because the two rules contradict each other
quiz.explanation: authorizeHttpRequests tries its rules from top to bottom and the first match decides. /** matches /admin/users, so authenticated() lets any signed-in user through and the admin rule is never consulted. Being more specific gives no precedence, and overlapping rules do not fail startup; only a rule added after anyRequest() does. Put specific matchers first.

quiz.prompt: A user is granted the authority `ADMIN`, and the rule is `hasRole("ADMIN")`. What is the result?
choices: Allowed: hasRole and hasAuthority check the same thing
Denied: hasRole looks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN
Allowed, because the ROLE_ prefix is optional in a check
The app fails at startup: authorities need the prefix
quiz.explanation: hasRole("ADMIN") adds the ROLE_ prefix and looks for the granted authority ROLE_ADMIN, so a user holding plain ADMIN is denied. hasAuthority is the check that compares the exact string; the prefix is not optional in hasRole, and nothing fails at startup. Grant ROLE_ADMIN, or write hasAuthority("ADMIN").

quiz.prompt: An `authenticated()` rule refuses an anonymous request on an API that uses bearer tokens. What does ExceptionTranslationFilter send?
choices: 403 Forbidden, from the AccessDeniedHandler
A 302 redirect to the login page, in every case
500, because nothing handled the exception
401 with WWW-Authenticate, from the entry point
quiz.explanation: The caller is anonymous, so ExceptionTranslationFilter treats the AccessDeniedException as authentication required and calls the AuthenticationEntryPoint, not the AccessDeniedHandler that would send 403. A bearer-token resource server's entry point answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer challenge; a redirect to the login page is what the form-login entry point does instead.

quiz.prompt: A signed-in user lacks the role an endpoint needs. Which component answers, and with what?
choices: The AuthenticationEntryPoint, with a 401 challenge
The AccessDeniedHandler, with 403
The controller advice, with a 400 Bad Request
The CSRF filter, with a 419 status of its own
quiz.explanation: The caller is already authenticated, so signing in again would not help: ExceptionTranslationFilter passes the AccessDeniedException to the AccessDeniedHandler, which answers 403. The entry point and its 401 challenge are for anonymous callers only. A URL rule refuses the request while it is still in the security filters, so a controller advice never sees it and cannot turn it into a 400.

quiz.prompt: A service hands work to a plain thread-pool executor, and that work reads `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()`. What does it see?
choices: The request's user, because the context is global
No authentication: the context is thread-local by default
The user who last used that pool thread for a request
An anonymous token that the executor created for it
quiz.explanation: SecurityContextHolder keeps the context per thread by default, so the work on a pool thread sees an empty context and getAuthentication() returns null. The context is not global, and the pool thread holds no earlier request's user, because it never served a request and request threads are cleared when the request ends. Propagate the context on purpose with DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor.

quiz.prompt: `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` sits on `deleteAll()`. Another method of the same bean calls `this.deleteAll()` for an ordinary user. What happens?
choices: AccessDeniedException, as for any other caller
It runs: a call on this skips the security proxy
Spring rewrites the call to go through the proxy
The app fails at startup because of the self-call
quiz.explanation: @PreAuthorize is enforced by a proxy around the bean, and this.deleteAll() calls the target object directly, so the check never runs and the ordinary user deletes everything. Spring does not rewrite self-calls, nothing fails at startup, and no AccessDeniedException is thrown. Move the method to another bean when internal calls must be checked, exactly as with @Transactional.

quiz.prompt: A cookie-session app receives a form POST without the CSRF token. What is the response?
choices: 403 Forbidden: CSRF protection rejects it
200, because CSRF only applies to GET requests
401, so that the user signs in all over again
A 302 back to the form, carrying an error message
quiz.explanation: CSRF protection is on by default in every chain HttpSecurity builds and guards the state-changing methods POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. A form POST without the token is refused with 403 Forbidden by the CSRF filter. It is not a 401, because the session itself is valid, and GET requests are exactly the ones CSRF leaves alone.

quiz.prompt: Why can a stateless API that reads a bearer token from the `Authorization` header usually disable CSRF protection?
choices: Bearer tokens are encrypted, so nobody can forge them
A browser never adds that header to a cross-site request
CSRF only applies to HTML forms, never to JSON bodies
Spring checks the Origin header of every API call anyway
quiz.explanation: CSRF abuses credentials the browser attaches automatically, such as cookies. A header the page's own code must add cannot be sent by a forged cross-site form.

quiz.prompt: Two SecurityFilterChain beans exist: one with `securityMatcher("/api/**")`, ordered first, and one with no matcher. How is a request to `/api/orders` handled?
choices: Both chains run, one after the other
The chain with no matcher always takes precedence
Only the first chain whose matcher fits it
Spring merges the two chains' rules into one list
quiz.explanation: FilterChainProxy picks exactly one SecurityFilterChain per request: the first, in order, whose matcher fits. /api/orders matches the API chain, so its filters alone run and the chain with no matcher is never consulted. Chains are not merged and do not run one after the other; the catch-all chain only handles what the earlier ones did not match.

flashcards.back: An ordered list of security filters for the requests its matcher selects; FilterChainProxy runs the first matching chain before the servlet.

flashcards.front: How does authorizeHttpRequests pick a rule?
flashcards.back: In declaration order: the earliest rule that fits the path and method wins, so specific paths go first and anyRequest() goes last.
hasRole("X") prepends the ROLE_ prefix before comparing; hasAuthority("X") compares the string exactly as it was granted.

flashcards.front: Where does the current user live?
flashcards.back: In the SecurityContextHolder. Its default strategy keeps one context per thread, and the framework clears it when the request ends.
The AuthenticationEntryPoint starts authentication (401 or a login redirect); the AccessDeniedHandler refuses a known caller (403).

flashcards.front: Access denied for an anonymous caller
flashcards.back: ExceptionTranslationFilter treats it as "authentication required" and calls the entry point rather than the access-denied handler.
@EnableMethodSecurity plus @PreAuthorize on bean methods, enforced by a proxy, so a call on this inside the bean is not checked.
On for state-changing requests with cookie sessions: a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE without the token is refused.

topics.title: Jackson: JSON contracts that survive change
topics.summary: How Jackson names JSON keys, unknown properties in plain Jackson versus Spring Boot, absent versus null versus defaults, dates and money on the wire, enums that evolve, why entities are the wrong contract, and which contract changes old readers and old writers survive.
topics.lesson:
## The JSON is a contract, not your class

```java
public record OrderResponse(
    @JsonProperty("id") String id,
    @JsonProperty("total") BigDecimal total,
    @JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL) String note,
    Instant createdAt) {}
```

Jackson builds the JSON keys from the Java names it finds: public getters and fields, and the components of a record (bound through its canonical constructor since Jackson 2.12). Rename the Java field `total` to `amount` and the wire key changes with it, so every client that reads `total` breaks at once. `@JsonProperty` pins the external name and lets the Java name change freely. Treat the response and request DTOs as published API: separate classes from your entities, reviewed like any other interface.

## Unknown properties: strict by default, tolerant in Spring Boot

A plain `new ObjectMapper()` has `DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES` on: a body with a key the class does not declare throws `UnrecognizedPropertyException`. Spring Boot's auto-configured mapper turns that feature off, so the same key is skipped without a word. Tolerance lets servers add response fields without breaking clients (the tolerant reader). It also means a misspelled field in a request, `emial`, is silently dropped, so a PATCH that matters should check its keys on purpose.

## Missing, null and the default value

A key that is absent leaves a field at its Java default: `null` for objects, `0` or `false` for primitives. An explicit `null` for an `int` also becomes `0` unless `FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES` is on. So a body without `quantity` binds to `quantity == 0` with no error; use `Integer` plus validation when "not sent" must be refused. A DTO field cannot tell `{}` from `{"phone": null}` either: both leave `null`. A PATCH that must clear some fields and keep others reads the body as a `Map` or `JsonNode` and asks `containsKey`. On the way out, `@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)` drops null fields, so readers must treat a missing key and a null value alike.

## Dates, money and numbers

`java.time` types need the `JavaTimeModule`; Spring Boot registers it and turns off `WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS`, so an `Instant` goes out as an ISO-8601 string such as `"2026-03-07T10:00:00Z"`. A bare `ObjectMapper` with the module writes a number of seconds instead. Money as a JSON number with decimals is risky: many clients parse every number as a binary double, and Jackson itself reads a decimal into a `double` when the target is untyped (a `Map` or `Object`) unless `USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS` is set. Send amounts as integer minor units (`"totalCents": 1999`) or as a decimal string with its currency.

## Enums evolve too

An enum is written as its `name()`. Reading a value the enum does not have, say a new `"REFUNDED"` status, throws `InvalidFormatException` by default, in plain Jackson and in Spring Boot alike. Renaming a constant is a breaking change on the wire. Clients that must survive new values mark a fallback constant with `@JsonEnumDefaultValue` and enable `READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_USING_DEFAULT_VALUE`.

## Never serialize entities

An entity is the wrong contract: it exposes columns such as `passwordHash`, it changes whenever the schema does, and its relations fight the serializer. A bidirectional `Order` / `OrderLine` pair recurses order, lines, order, until Jackson fails with an infinite-recursion error, and a lazy collection either fires extra queries while the response is written (open-in-view) or, with open-in-view off, throws `LazyInitializationException` (topic 20). Map entities to DTOs inside the service.

## Change a contract in a way old clients survive

Ask who reads and who writes. For a response, adding an optional field is safe for tolerant readers; removing or renaming a field that was always present, changing its type, or letting it go missing breaks them. For a request, a new required field breaks every old client that does not send it, while a new optional field does not. Expand first (add the new name, keep the old), migrate the clients, then contract.

quiz.prompt: A plain `new ObjectMapper()` reads `{"id": 7, "nickname": "x"}` into a class that declares only `id`. What happens?
choices: nickname is skipped and id is read as 7
It throws UnrecognizedPropertyException
nickname is stored in a hidden map on the object
id is read and nickname becomes a null field
quiz.explanation: A bare ObjectMapper has FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES on, so a key the class does not declare stops the read with an exception. Skipping the key silently is what Spring Boot's auto-configured mapper does, because it turns that feature off. Jackson never invents a field or a hidden map unless the class asks for one with @JsonAnySetter.

quiz.prompt: A PATCH body in a Spring Boot app arrives as `{"emial": "ana@new.io"}`, a typo for `email`. With the default mapper and a DTO, what happens?
choices: The request fails with a 400 for the unknown key
Spring maps it to email by the closest field name
The server returns 500 because the bind fails
The key is skipped and the email does not change
quiz.explanation: Spring Boot's mapper disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, so the misspelled key is dropped without a word and the handler sees an empty patch. That tolerance helps clients survive new response fields, but on a PATCH it hides mistakes; nothing guesses the closest name. Check the keys on purpose when a silent no-op would hurt.

quiz.prompt: A request body omits `quantity`, and the DTO declares `int quantity`. What does the bound object hold?
choices: 0, with no error: the field keeps its default
null, until a validator rejects the missing value
The bind fails with a missing-property error
-1, which Jackson uses for missing numbers
quiz.explanation: An absent key is never written, so the primitive keeps its Java default of 0, and Jackson raises no missing-property error by default. An int cannot hold null, so @NotNull cannot catch it either. Declare Integer and validate it when not sending a quantity must be refused instead of meaning zero.

quiz.prompt: A developer renames the DTO record component `total` to `amount`. There is no annotation. What do existing clients see?
choices: Nothing changes: Jackson keeps the old key name
Jackson writes both total and amount for one release
The key becomes amount; readers of total break
The app fails at startup until a mapping is added
quiz.explanation: Jackson derives the wire name from the Java name, so the rename quietly changes the contract and every client that reads total gets nothing. No release writes both keys and nothing fails at startup. Pin the external name with @JsonProperty("total"), or expand and contract: add amount, keep total until the clients move.

quiz.prompt: In a Spring Boot app, a response DTO has an `Instant createdAt`. What does the JSON hold?
choices: A number of milliseconds since the epoch, as a long
An ISO-8601 string such as "2026-03-07T10:00:00Z"
An object with seconds and nanos fields
Nothing, because Jackson cannot write Instant
quiz.explanation: Spring Boot registers the JavaTimeModule and turns off WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS, so an Instant goes out as an ISO-8601 string. A bare ObjectMapper with the module writes a numeric timestamp instead, and one without the module refuses java.time types. The output never becomes an object of seconds and nanos.

quiz.prompt: The server adds the status `REFUNDED`. A Java client whose `Status` enum lacks it reads a refunded order with default settings. What happens?
choices: status is set to null and the read goes on
The read succeeds with the first enum constant
The unknown value is kept as a plain string
The read fails with InvalidFormatException
quiz.explanation: Jackson refuses an enum value it cannot map, by default in plain Jackson and in Spring Boot. Reading it as null needs READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_AS_NULL, and a fallback constant needs @JsonEnumDefaultValue plus its feature. A new enum value is therefore a breaking change for strict clients, just like a removed field.

quiz.prompt: A controller returns an `Order` entity whose `lines` each point back to their `order`. There are no Jackson annotations. What happens when the response is written?
choices: Jackson writes each order once and skips the cycle
It recurses order, lines, order until it fails
The lines are left out because they are lazy
Spring converts the entity to a DTO on its own
quiz.explanation: Jackson follows every getter, so order leads to lines, each line back to order, and the recursion ends in an infinite-recursion error. It does not detect the cycle by itself, and Spring never converts entities to DTOs. Map to a DTO inside the service; @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference only patch the symptom.

quiz.prompt: A PATCH DTO has a `String phone` field. How can the handler tell `{}` (keep the phone) from `{"phone": null}` (clear it)?
choices: Check whether phone is null after binding
Mark the field @JsonInclude(NON_NULL)
It cannot: both leave phone null
Jackson sets phone to an empty string for null
quiz.explanation: An absent key and an explicit null both leave the field null, so a null check cannot separate keep from clear. @JsonInclude affects writing, not reading, and Jackson never swaps null for an empty string. Read the body as a Map or JsonNode and ask containsKey, or use a wrapper type that records whether a field was sent.

quiz.prompt: Why send a price as integer cents (`"totalCents": 1999`) or a decimal string rather than `"total": 19.99`?
choices: Many clients parse JSON numbers as doubles
JSON has no syntax for numbers with a decimal point
Jackson cannot write a BigDecimal as a JSON number
Integers make the response body much smaller
quiz.explanation: JSON can carry 19.99, and Jackson writes BigDecimal as a number, but many readers, including JavaScript and a Jackson read into a double field or an untyped Map, turn it into a binary float that cannot hold most cents exactly. Size is not the issue. Integer minor units or a decimal string keep the amount exact on every client.

quiz.prompt: A response DTO marks `note` with `@JsonInclude(Include.NON_NULL)`, and the order has no note. What does a client receive?
choices: note set to the empty string
"note": null in the object
The note key is left out of the object
An error, because note is required
quiz.explanation: NON_NULL drops a property whose value is null, so the object has no note key at all rather than "note": null or an empty string. Nothing fails, because the annotation only shapes output. Clients must then treat a missing key and a null value the same way, which is worth saying in the API docs.

flashcards.front: Where do Jackson's JSON key names come from?
flashcards.back: From the Java names it finds: public getters and fields and record components. @JsonProperty pins an external name so the Java name can change.

flashcards.front: FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, plain Jackson versus Spring Boot
flashcards.back: A bare ObjectMapper turns an undeclared key into an error; Spring Boot's mapper switches the feature off and skips such keys.
A client that ignores keys it does not know, so a server can add response fields without a coordinated release.

flashcards.front: Absent key versus explicit null in a DTO
flashcards.back: Both leave an object field null; a PATCH that must tell them apart reads a Map or JsonNode and checks containsKey.
Boot registers the JavaTimeModule and writes dates as ISO-8601 strings, not numeric timestamps.
Integer minor units or a decimal string plus currency, never a float that every client may parse as a binary double.

flashcards.front: A new enum value on the server
flashcards.back: Breaking for strict readers; a client survives it with @JsonEnumDefaultValue and the matching read feature, or by reading the value as text.
Safe: add an optional response field, add an optional request field. Unsafe: remove, rename or retype a field, or add a required request field.

topics.title: Bean Validation in depth: null rules, cascading, groups, errors
topics.summary: Where constraints live and when they run, NotNull versus NotEmpty versus NotBlank, why null passes every other constraint, @Valid cascading into nested objects and list elements, method validation through a proxy, custom and cross-field constraints, groups and Default, and a 400 body that helps without leaking secrets.

quiz.prompt: A DTO has `@Size(min = 2, max = 40) String name`. The request body has no `name` at all. What does validation report?
choices: A size violation, since null has no length
Nothing: Size treats null as valid
A NullPointerException inside the validator
A 500, because the field could not be bound
quiz.explanation: Every built-in constraint except the NotNull family treats null as valid, so Size has nothing to check and the request passes. That is deliberate: each annotation checks one property. A required name needs @NotBlank or @NotNull next to @Size; the validator neither throws nor turns a missing field into a size violation.

quiz.prompt: Which constraint refuses `null`, `""` and `"   "` for a String field?
choices: @NotNull
@NotEmpty
@Size(min = 1)
@NotBlank
quiz.explanation: @NotBlank refuses null and any string whose trimmed content is empty. @NotEmpty refuses null and the empty string but accepts three spaces, @NotNull accepts both empty forms, and @Size(min = 1) passes null and counts spaces as characters. Pick @NotBlank for names and other text a person must actually type.

quiz.prompt: A controller method takes `@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder body`, and the body breaks two constraints. What happens?
choices: Spring refuses it with 400 before the handler
The method runs with body.errors() filled in
Only the first violation is reported, as a 422
Spring drops the invalid fields and goes on
quiz.explanation: Spring validates the bound body before calling the method and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which the default handling turns into a 400. Both violations are collected, not only the first, and the method never runs with a half-valid object. Fields are never dropped silently, and the default status is 400, not 422.

quiz.prompt: `CreateOrder` holds `Address shipTo` without `@Valid`; `Address.city` is `@NotBlank`. A request has `"city": ""`. What does validating `CreateOrder` report?
choices: shipTo.city: must not be blank
A violation on shipTo itself
Nothing: Address is not validated
An error, because Address needs @Validated
quiz.explanation: Validation does not cascade into a nested object unless the reference is marked @Valid, so the blank city is never looked at and no path is reported. @Validated is for Spring proxies and groups, not for cascading. Mark the component @Valid, and the violation appears with the path shipTo.city.

quiz.prompt: A bean is annotated `@Validated`; its public `register(@Email String email)` is called as `this.register(...)` from another method of the same bean. Is the email checked?
choices: Yes, the annotation is on the method
Only when assertions are enabled
Yes, but the violation is only logged
No: the call skips the validating proxy
quiz.explanation: Method validation is applied by a proxy around the bean, and a call on this goes straight to the target object, so no check runs at all. It is the same trap as @Transactional and @PreAuthorize. Assertions and logging play no part; call through another bean, or validate at the edge.

quiz.prompt: A DTO declares `@NotNull int quantity`, and the client omits quantity. What does the server see?
choices: quantity is 0 and passes
A NotNull violation for quantity
A JSON parse error
quantity is null in the DTO
quiz.explanation: A primitive cannot be null, so the missing value binds to 0 and @NotNull has nothing to refuse. The JSON is valid and no parse error occurs. Use Integer with @NotNull when sending the field is required, or @Min(1) when zero is not a legal quantity, so the bad request is caught.

quiz.prompt: You write a `@PostalCode` constraint. What should its `ConstraintValidator.isValid` return for `null`?
choices: false, since null is not a postal code
true, and leave required to @NotNull
It should throw IllegalArgumentException
It depends on the country being checked
quiz.explanation: The convention for every built-in constraint is that null is valid and presence is a separate rule. Returning false would make the field silently required, and throwing from a validator turns a bad request into a 500. Follow the convention so @PostalCode can sit on optional fields and combine with @NotNull where needed.

quiz.prompt: `id` has `@NotNull(groups = OnUpdate.class)`, `name` has a plain `@NotBlank`, and the controller uses `@Validated(OnUpdate.class)`. Which checks run?
choices: Both, because groups only add rules
name only, because id is not in Default
Neither: groups need a group sequence
Only id: name is in the Default group
quiz.explanation: A constraint without a group belongs to Default, and validating only OnUpdate checks only the OnUpdate constraints, so the blank name gets through. Groups do not add to Default unless OnUpdate extends Default, and no group sequence is needed for a single group. Two small DTOs often avoid the confusion.

quiz.prompt: A start date must be before an end date in the same booking. Where does that rule belong?
choices: In a class-level constraint on the booking
In @Past on the start date
Inside the JSON deserializer
In a database trigger only
quiz.explanation: A rule over two fields needs a validator that sees the whole object, which is what a class-level constraint gets. @Past compares one field with now, not with another field. A deserializer should only build the object, and a trigger alone reports the problem as a database error long after the request should have been refused.

quiz.prompt: A signup request breaks `@Size(min = 12)` on `password`. What should the 400 body include for that field?
choices: The message and the rejected password
Only a generic "bad request" with no fields
The message, never the rejected value
The message and the value, base64-encoded
quiz.explanation: The client needs to know which field failed and why, so the message belongs in the body, but a password must never be echoed: response bodies end up in logs, proxies and screenshots. Base64 is not protection. A generic error without fields hides what the user has to fix.

flashcards.back: Every constraint except @NotNull, @NotEmpty and @NotBlank accepts null, so presence and format are two separate annotations.
Not null at all; not null and length or size above zero; for text, not null and containing a non-whitespace character.
Mark a nested object or the element type of a collection with @Valid; violations then carry paths like lines[2].quantity.
Spring validates after binding and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, answered with 400, before the handler runs.
@Validated beans are checked by a proxy, so constraints on a method called through this are skipped.
Treat null as valid, keep it fast and pure, and leave lookups that need the database to the service.
Constraints without groups are in Default; validating another group checks only that group unless it extends Default.
Status 400, a stable title, messages per field; echo rejected values only for fields that are not secrets.

topics.title: SLF4J and the MDC: log lines you can follow
topics.summary: Parameterised SLF4J messages and why they are cheap when disabled, the trailing exception, logging once at the right level, a request id in the MDC set at the edge and cleared in finally, carrying the MDC into pool threads, refusing forged ids, and keeping secrets out of logs.

quiz.prompt: Debug logging is off. Which statement still builds a string and calls `summarize(order)`?
choices: log.debug("order {}", order)
log.debug("order " + summarize(order))
if (log.isDebugEnabled()) log.debug("order {}", summarize(order))
log.debug("order {} {}", order, 1)
quiz.explanation: Java evaluates the argument before calling debug, so the concatenation and summarize run even though the line is then dropped. The parameterised forms only pass references and call toString when the level is on, and the isDebugEnabled guard skips summarize entirely. Use placeholders for cheap values and a guard for costly ones.

quiz.prompt: What does `log.error("could not capture payment {}", paymentId, e)` print, where `e` is an exception?
choices: The message with e.toString() in place of {}
The message with paymentId, and e with its stack trace
Only the stack trace, without the message
Nothing: two arguments need two {}
quiz.explanation: The placeholder takes paymentId, and SLF4J treats the trailing Throwable as the exception to log, so the stack trace follows the message. Nothing is dropped, and a mismatch between arguments and placeholders is not an error. Concatenating the exception into the text instead would lose its stack trace.

quiz.prompt: A service catches an exception, logs it at ERROR and rethrows it; the controller logs it again; so does a filter. What is the problem?
choices: SLF4J refuses to log one exception twice
The stack trace is lost on the second log
The rethrow changes the exception type
One failure shows up as three errors
quiz.explanation: Each layer that logs and rethrows adds a copy, so one failure looks like three and alerts or dashboards count it three times. SLF4J does not stop duplicates, and rethrowing keeps both the type and the stack trace. Log where the exception is handled, and let the others add context by wrapping it with a cause.

quiz.prompt: A payment provider timed out, and the retry succeeded. Which level fits that event?
choices: WARN: degraded, but handled
ERROR, because a call failed
DEBUG, since the user saw nothing
INFO, as a business event
quiz.explanation: The system degraded and recovered on its own, which is what WARN is for: worth seeing in aggregate, no one needs to act right now. ERROR would page someone for a handled event, DEBUG is usually off in production so the pattern would vanish, and the payment itself is the business event, not the timeout.

quiz.prompt: A filter copies the raw `X-Request-Id` header into the MDC. Why is that risky?
choices: The MDC only accepts numeric values
Request ids must be generated by the server
A header with a newline can forge log lines
Headers are not readable inside filters
quiz.explanation: A caller controls that header, and a value with a newline and fake fields writes lines that look like they came from the server. The MDC takes any string, and a client-supplied id is useful for tracing if it is checked. Accept it only when it matches a strict pattern, otherwise generate one.

quiz.prompt: A filter calls `MDC.put("requestId", id)` and then the chain, but has no `finally`. The chain throws. What happens next on that thread?
choices: The servlet container clears the MDC for you
The id stays and labels the next request
The exception removes the MDC entry
The next MDC.put fails with an error
quiz.explanation: The MDC is a thread-local map, and pooled server threads serve many requests, so an entry that is not removed stays behind and tags the next request's lines with the wrong id. Neither the container nor the exception clears it, and a later put simply overwrites. Remove it in finally, or use MDC.putCloseable.

quiz.prompt: A request handler submits work to an `ExecutorService`. What request id does the task's log line carry?
choices: The handler's id, because MDC is inherited
The id of the first request the pool served
Whatever the worker thread has, often none
An id the executor generates for each task
quiz.explanation: The MDC belongs to a thread, and pool threads are not children of the request thread, so the task sees the worker's own context, usually empty. Nothing is inherited or generated per task. Capture the context map when the task is created and install it around the task, for example with a TaskDecorator.

quiz.prompt: When should a task wrapper read `MDC.getCopyOfContextMap()`?
choices: When the task is created, on the caller's thread
When the task starts, on the worker thread
After the task ends, to restore it
Never: setContextMap copies it for you
quiz.explanation: Only the caller's thread holds the request's context, so the copy must be taken when the task is created. Reading it when the task starts gives the worker's context, which is the bug the wrapper exists to fix. The worker's own map is read separately at that point so it can be put back afterwards.

quiz.prompt: `log.info("login attempt {}", credentials)` logs a record `Credentials(user, password)`. What is printed by default?
choices: Only the class name of the object
The user and the password, from the record's toString
A masked password, because SLF4J hides fields
Nothing until a toString is written
quiz.explanation: The placeholder calls toString, and a record's generated toString prints every component, password included. SLF4J does not inspect or mask fields, and a record always has a toString. Override toString on types that carry secrets, and prefer logging an id over the object.

quiz.prompt: What does `log.info("set \\{} has {} items", 3)` print?
choices: set 3 has {} items
An error: escapes are not supported
set {} has {} items
set {} has 3 items
quiz.explanation: A backslash before a placeholder escapes it, so the first {} is printed literally and does not use an argument; the 3 goes to the second one. Without the escape the 3 would fill the first placeholder, and the backslash itself is not printed. Escapes are supported, so there is no error; a double backslash would print one backslash and then substitute.

flashcards.back: The message is formatted only when the level is enabled, so a disabled debug line costs almost nothing.

flashcards.front: Where does the exception go in an SLF4J call?
flashcards.back: After the values for every {}; a trailing Throwable is printed with its stack trace.
Each layer that does it duplicates the failure; log where it is handled and wrap with a cause elsewhere.
A per-thread map of context, such as a request id, that the log pattern prints on every line.
Put at the edge, remove in finally, or the entry labels the next request served by that thread.
Copy the context where the task is created, install it around the task, then restore the worker's own.
Only when it matches a strict format; otherwise generate one, since raw headers can forge log lines.
Never: log ids not payloads, mask what must appear, and keep toString of credential types safe.

topics.title: HTTP clients: timeouts, retries and deadline budgets
topics.summary: Why java.net.http waits for ever without a timeout, connect versus request timeouts, slow dependencies and bulkheads, which methods and failures may be retried, exponential backoff with jitter and Retry-After, retry amplification across layers, deadline budgets, and testing timeouts without waiting.
topics.lesson:
## No timeout means wait for ever

```java
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NEVER)
    .build();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://prices.internal/v1/sku/42"))
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(800))
    .GET()
    .build();

HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
```

`java.net.http.HttpClient` (JDK 11+) has no request timeout unless you set one: the javadoc says leaving it out is the same as an infinite duration. `connectTimeout` bounds the TCP and TLS setup; `HttpRequest.timeout` makes `send` throw `HttpTimeoutException` (and `sendAsync` complete exceptionally with it) when the response does not arrive in time. Spring's older `RestTemplate` on its default request factory also waits indefinitely. Set both timeouts on every client, deliberately, per dependency.

## A slow dependency is worse than a dead one

A dead service fails fast; a slow one holds a thread, a connection and the user's request for as long as you let it. With 200 request threads and a dependency that answers in 30 s, a burst of traffic parks every thread on it. Short timeouts, a bulkhead (a cap on concurrent calls) and a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency keep one bad service from taking the rest down.

## Retry only what is safe to repeat

GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition (RFC 9110): doing them twice has the effect of doing them once. A POST is not, unless the server deduplicates it by an idempotency key. A connect timeout is safe to retry for any method, because nothing reached the server; a request timeout is not, because the server may have done the work and only the answer was lost.

## Retry only what may succeed next time

Retry 429 (too many requests), 502, 503, 504 and transport failures. Do not retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or 409: the same request will get the same answer. A plain 500 is usually a bug on the other side, not a blip, so many clients do not retry it either.

## Back off, add jitter, honour Retry-After

Wait before each retry, doubling the wait each time up to a cap, and pick a random point below it ("full jitter") so a thousand clients do not retry in the same millisecond. When the server sends `Retry-After`, use it (capped at what you are willing to wait). Limit attempts, and count them across the whole call chain: three layers that each retry three times turn one failure into 27 calls.

## Budgets: the deadline belongs to the caller

The user's request has one deadline. Each outbound call gets the time that is LEFT, minus a small reserve for building the answer, and never more than its own cap. When too little is left to be useful, fail at once instead of starting a call that cannot finish. Passing the deadline on (a header such as `X-Deadline`) lets the next service stop work nobody is waiting for.

## Test timeouts without waiting for them

Inject a `Clock` and decide timeouts as plain values, then assert on `request.timeout()` and `client.connectTimeout()`: both are readable `Optional`s on the JDK objects. Keep real network tests few, against a local stub server, with timeouts in milliseconds.

quiz.prompt: An `HttpRequest` is built without `.timeout(...)` and sent with `client.send`. The server accepts the connection and never answers. What happens?
choices: send throws HttpTimeoutException after the JDK default of 30 s
send blocks for as long as the server stays silent
send throws at once with HttpTimeoutException
send returns a 504 response it makes up itself
quiz.explanation: Leaving out the request timeout is the same as an infinite one, so send keeps waiting for a response that never comes. There is no hidden 30-second default, the client never invents a 504, and an immediate exception would need a timeout that was set. Set a per-request timeout on every call to a dependency.

quiz.prompt: What does `HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))` bound?
choices: Setting up the connection only
The whole call, from connect to the last body byte
Only the TLS handshake, after TCP connects
The time between two chunks of the response body
quiz.explanation: connectTimeout covers establishing the connection; once it is up, how long the response may take is the request's own timeout. It does not bound the whole call or the gaps between body chunks, and it is not limited to the TLS part. Set both, because a connected but slow server is the common case.

quiz.prompt: A POST to create a payment times out after the request was sent. Should the client retry it as is?
choices: Yes, a timeout means the server never saw it
Yes, but only after waiting the full backoff
No, because POST bodies cannot be sent twice
No, not without an idempotency key
quiz.explanation: A request timeout means the answer did not arrive, not that the work did not happen, so a blind retry can charge twice. Waiting longer does not change that, and a body can technically be sent again. With an idempotency key the server returns the first result instead of acting twice, which makes the retry safe.

quiz.prompt: Which failure is safe to retry even for a POST without an idempotency key?
choices: A read timeout after the whole body was sent
A connect timeout: nothing reached the server
A 503 Service Unavailable from the load balancer
A 409 Conflict answer from the payment provider API
quiz.explanation: When the connection never came up, no request reached the server, so repeating it cannot duplicate anything. After a read timeout or a 503 the request did arrive and may have run, and a 409 is a definite answer that a retry will only repeat. Treat transport failures by when they happened, not by their name.

quiz.prompt: Which response is NOT worth retrying?
choices: 429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable
404 Not Found
504 Gateway Timeout
quiz.explanation: A 404 is a definite answer about the resource, and asking again gets the same answer, so retrying only adds load. 429, 503 and 504 describe a temporary condition on the server or a proxy, which may clear in a moment, ideally after the wait the server suggests in Retry-After.

quiz.prompt: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
choices: So that many clients do not retry at the same moment
Because servers reject requests that are evenly spaced
To make the total wait shorter than plain doubling
So that the backoff never reaches its cap
quiz.explanation: Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together, hitting the recovering server with synchronised waves. Jitter spreads them out. Servers do not reject regular spacing, full jitter usually waits less only on average, and the cap still applies. Pick a random delay under the current ceiling.

quiz.prompt: A 429 response carries `Retry-After: 2`. Your backoff would wait 100 ms. What should the client do?
choices: Wait 100 ms: the client controls its own backoff
Retry at once, since 429 means try again
Give up, because 429 is a client error
Wait about 2 seconds, as the server asked
quiz.explanation: Retry-After is the server telling you when capacity will be back, so it overrides your own guess, within a cap you choose. Retrying sooner earns another 429 and adds to the overload, and 429 is precisely the 4xx that is meant to be retried later. Retry-After in seconds is the common form.

quiz.prompt: The gateway retries 3 times, the service behind it retries 3 times, and its database client retries 3 times. One request hits a failing database. How many database calls can that cause?
choices: 3, because only the database client retries it
9, two layers of three
Up to 27, three layers of three
1, since retries are deduplicated
quiz.explanation: Each layer repeats everything beneath it, so three layers of three attempts multiply to 27 calls for one user request. Nothing deduplicates them, and the gateway's retries repeat the service's retries too. Retry in one layer, usually the one closest to the failure, and give the others a budget.

quiz.prompt: A request must finish within 300 ms and 250 ms are already spent. The price call normally gets 800 ms. What timeout should it get?
choices: 800 ms, its usual per-call setting
About 30 ms, the rest minus a reserve, or none
300 ms, the full deadline of the incoming request
No timeout at all, to give the call its best chance
quiz.explanation: Only 50 ms are left, and part of that is needed to build the answer, so the call gets the small remainder, or none at all when that is too little to be useful. 800 ms or 300 ms would outlive the caller, who has already given up, and no timeout means waiting for ever. Budgets flow from the caller's deadline.

quiz.prompt: How can a unit test check that a request is built with an 800 ms timeout without sending it?
choices: Send it to a server that sleeps for 801 ms
Mock HttpClient and capture the arguments of its send call
It cannot: the timeout is private to the request
Assert request.timeout() equals Optional.of(800 ms)
quiz.explanation: HttpRequest exposes its timeout as an Optional, so building the request with an injected clock and asserting on that value tests the decision directly. A sleeping server makes the test slow and timing-dependent, and mocking HttpClient tests the mock. The value is public, so nothing is hidden.

flashcards.back: Leaving it out equals an infinite duration, so a silent server holds the calling thread indefinitely.
One bounds establishing the connection, the other the wait for the response; set both per dependency.

flashcards.front: Which methods may be retried as they are?
flashcards.back: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE; a POST only with an idempotency key the server honours.

flashcards.front: Connect timeout versus read timeout, for retries
flashcards.back: Before connecting nothing reached the server; after sending, the work may already have happened.

flashcards.front: Which statuses are worth a retry?
flashcards.back: 429, 502, 503 and 504; other 4xx answers will repeat, and a plain 500 is usually a bug.
Double the ceiling each attempt up to a cap, and wait a random time under it so clients spread out.
Layers that each retry multiply their attempts; retry in one layer and budget the rest.
Give each call the time left minus a reserve, capped; fail fast when too little remains, and pass the deadline on.
